title: You know the launch market is tough when satellite companies start building rockets
gist: AST SpaceMobile announced Blacklift, a 20-ton medium-lift rocket it says will launch commercially in late 2028, backed by a $1.3B Firefly engine deal; Eric Berger calls the timeline wildly optimistic versus a 5-9 year historical norm. He argues the move reflects a worsening launch-capacity crunch and investor appetite for medium-lift entrants, while questioning why AST needs it given existing contracts for 100+ satellites.

insights.claim: Satellite operators deploying large constellations need to secure launch capacity years in advance, and those unable to get favorable terms are now considering building their own rockets.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Launch scarcity confers pricing power on incumbents like SpaceX and pushes constellation operators toward vertical integration.

insights.claim: Investors recognizing the worsening launch crisis are making capital available for new medium-lift launch entrants, such as Cowboy Space's Big Iron, also claimed to fly in 2028.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Capital is flowing into launch startups with aggressive claims, a potential bubble signal.

insights.claim: Of the US medium-to-heavy rockets announced since 2015, only ULA's Vulcan has reached orbit, after 8.7 years and about $2 billion in aggregate federal support.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: New launch vehicles are slow and expensive; Rocket Lab, Relativity, Firefly and Stoke still face execution risk.

insights.claim: AST committed $1.3 billion to Firefly: $800 million for a perpetual Miranda/Vira engine license, $250 million for 27 Miranda and nine Vira engines, and $250 million for engineering support.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
